title: Minimum potential energy plus proportional growth yields the logarithmic spiral

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Minimum potential energy plus proportional growth yields the logarithmic spiral

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Each new protoplasmic drop settles in a position of minimum potential energy (including minimal area), which makes each chamber similar to the last; proportional growth of size then gives the series the form of a logarithmic spiral. Rhumbler's specific 'law of the constant angle' of contact is too narrow an explanation.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XII: The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The physical law of minimum potential (including also the law of minimal area) is all that we need in order to explain, _in general terms_, the continued similarity of one chamber to another; and the physiological law of growth, by which a continued proportionality of size tends to run through the series of successive chambers, impresses upon this series of similar increments the form of a logarithmic spiral.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XII, “The Spiral Shells of the Foraminifera”; topic “Minimum potential and chamber similarity”. Scope: chambered Foraminifera

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch12-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.39

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim can be translated into physical models, but its broad minimum-potential wording permits many parameterizations. Static morphology offers only partial discrimination among the proposed and rival mechanisms.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit minimum-energy chamber-shape models and proportional-size spiral models jointly to segmented shell ontogenies, comparing them with models based on fixed contact angle and biologically specified secretion. Better predictive fit across taxa would support the compound mechanism; failure of either component would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Several mechanisms predict similar static chamber forms.

Potential energy and boundary conditions are not observed directly.

Open ontogenetic 3D series are limited.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim sets a minimal-area-plus-proportional-growth account against a narrower constant-angle rule, and both make geometric predictions that sections and scans can score. Energy itself is not observed, and the mapping from a finished calcareous wall back to a soft drop is an interpretation. With sparse 3D coverage, the model comparison is realistic for a few well-scanned genera and illustrative elsewhere.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For successive chambers, compare observed surfaces with area-minimizing surfaces on the previous aperture, record similarity after scaling, and test whether the contact angle is constant as Rhumbler claimed. The broader account is favored if chambers stay near minimal area and similar in shape even where the contact angle varies; it is weakened if a single contact angle predicts chamber form and minimal-area surfaces do not.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Potential energy is inferred from shape, so a minimal-area fit does not measure the forces that acted while the chamber was soft.

Only a small number of chambered species have open volumetric scans.
